paragraphs.heading: A green variety of beryl
paragraphs.text: Emerald is a gemstone, a variety of the mineral called beryl. Trace amounts of chromium, or sometimes vanadium, color it green. It ranks among the traditional "big four" precious gems, together with diamonds, rubies and sapphires. On the Mohs scale, beryl's hardness is 7.5–8.

paragraphs.heading: What makes the green
paragraphs.text: The trace elements behind emerald's color are chromium, vanadium and iron. Which of them are present, and in what relative amounts, decides the exact color of a crystal. Gemology divides color into three components: hue, saturation and tone. Emerald hues run from yellow-green to blue-green, and yellow and blue are the normal secondary hues. Only gems of medium to dark tone are considered emeralds; light-toned ones are known as green beryl instead.

paragraphs.heading: What the best ones look like
paragraphs.text: The finest emeralds sit at about 75% tone, on a scale where 0% is colorless and 100% is opaque black. A fine emerald is also well saturated, with a bright, vivid hue. Gray is the normal saturation modifier found in emeralds, and a grayish green hue is a dull green one. A top gemstone needs more than a pure green hue: it must also be highly transparent.

paragraphs.heading: The garden inside
paragraphs.text: Emeralds tend to have numerous inclusions and fissures that break the surface. Since most emeralds have many inclusions, their toughness is classified as poor. Diamonds have their clarity graded under 10× magnification, but emeralds are graded by eye. An emerald with no inclusions visible to the eye is considered flawless. The inclusions and fissures are sometimes called jardin, French for garden, because they look mossy. Each emerald's imperfections are unique, and they can serve to identify a particular stone.

paragraphs.heading: Oil in the cracks
paragraphs.text: Stones without surface-breaking fissures are extremely rare, and for that reason almost all emeralds are treated to make them look clearer. Most are oiled to fill cracks that reach the surface, which improves clarity and stability. Cedar oil, which has a similar refractive index, is often used. Epoxy resins are often used on the least expensive emeralds; they work well for filling stones with many fractures. These treatments are usually done in a vacuum chamber with mild heat, which opens the pores of the stone and lets the filler be absorbed more effectively.

paragraphs.heading: What the trade accepts
paragraphs.text: Oiling is traditional, and the gem trade largely accepts it, but an oil-treated emerald is worth much less than an untreated one of similar quality. The Federal Trade Commission requires the treatment to be disclosed when an oil-treated emerald is sold. Other treatments, such as green-tinted oil, are not acceptable in the trade. Enhancement is graded in four steps: none, minor, moderate and highly enhanced. These steps describe how much a stone has been enhanced, not how clear it is. A gem graded none may still show visible inclusions.

paragraphs.heading: Ancient mines
paragraphs.text: In antiquity, emeralds were dug in Ancient Egypt at sites on Mount Smaragdus from 1500 BC. The Roman and Byzantine Empires worked the Egyptian mines on an industrial scale, and Islamic conquerors did so later. Emeralds have also been mined in Austria and India since at least the 14th century AD.
